..(Friday Night through Wednesday)
Issued at 402 PM EST Wed Nov 25 2026

The long term forecast period opens in the wake of the well-
advertised late-week upper level low. The flow aloft looks to become 
more zonal on Saturday as shortwave ridging briefly builds back into 
the Ohio River Valley. This should yield a clearing and warming 
trend, but it remains uncertain how fast these trends will come to 
fruition. Any locations that clear out on Friday night could see 
lows below freezing on Saturday morning, and we may have to watch 
out for localized slick spots there given the antecedently wet 
grounds. Where clouds stick around at night, lows will likely remain 
insulated in the upper half of the 30s. Bias correction techniques 
appear to be skewing Friday night's MinT grids too cold, so CONS 
data was blended in to mitigate the idea of a widespread flash 
freeze. Given that this system won't feature a prolonged period of 
NW flow, that clearing trend should spread across the entire area on 
Saturday. Highs accordingly rebound into the 50s, with low-level 
warm air advection ramping up further ahead of the next storm system 
on Sunday. 

Sunday's setup is quite different than that upper-level low; it is a 
more traditional, but rather sharp, shortwave trough ejecting out of 
the Plains and into the Ohio River Valley. This morning's forecast 
guidance suite has come closer to a consensus on this feature's 
timing and magnitude, but I would like to see this persist for at 
least one more model cycle before jumping too far into the resultant 
sensible weather forecast details. In general, expect Eastern 
Kentucky to be firmly positioned on the warm side of this system, 
with deep southwesterly flow advecting ample moisture into the 
column. The amount of WAA that gets realized at the surface is to be 
determined, but this will play a significant role in determining 
whether or not the precipitation associated with Sunday's system 
comes in the form of a plain rain or perhaps some thunderstorms. 
Increasing cloud cover should limit the amount of diurnal heating 
and thus the amount of instability. If Sunday's highs outperform 
current expectations and instability falls on the higher side of the 
forecast envelope, a few rumbles of thunder cannot be ruled out. The 
system's rather robust kinematic profiles could yield sufficient 
shear for some more organized convection. This could turn into a 
high shear, (very) low CAPE setup if model trends persist. Some of 
the recent medium-range AI/ML convective guidance is beginning to 
pick up on this signal, but confidence is not currently high enough 
to message widespread thunderstorms. Rather, this second system is 
poised to bring about another round of highly-beneficial widespread 
weather. Between the two of them, we should be able to put a dent in 
any fall fire weather and localized drought concerns.

The rest of the long term forecast period looks rather mundane. The 
cold air advection on the backside of Sunday's system does not 
appear strong enough nor long enough to produce a changeover to snow 
on Sunday night. Temperatures will not be able to drop below 
freezing until the clouds fully clear out on Monday night. A surface 
high pressure system will have worked its way into the region by 
then, with zonal flow in place aloft. Such synoptics favor drier 
weather and seasonable temperatures, with ridge-valley splits likely 
at night. A weaker shortwave passing through the zonal flow regime 
could cause an increase in clouds around midweek, but it does not 
look deep enough to yield any meaningful low-level moisture return. 
So, December 2026 should start off on a dry note.
